# Hours, Output and the Pilot Problem: A Re-examination of the Halden Reduced-Hours Pilot

*Comment, Journal of Labour and Organisation Studies. K. Varga and T. Holm, Centre for Applied Labour Statistics.*

## Abstract

The Halden pilot reported that 61 organisations maintained output while cutting scheduled hours by 20%, implying a 23.4% gain in output per hour. Using the pilot's microdata, released under the Institute's data-sharing policy, we re-examine the result. Four problems, each documented below, account for most of the reported gain: attrition that was not random, a manager-reported output measure that overstates output relative to organisations' own records, an hours denominator that counts scheduled rather than actual time, and an unadjusted revenue comparison. Correcting the first three, the gain in output per hour falls from 23.4% to 10.8% in the subset of organisations where correction is possible. We then argue that the remaining gain is plausibly a novelty effect, and that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty.

## 1. Attrition

The working paper states that nine of the 70 enrolled organisations "withdrew during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons". The microdata tell a different story. Seven of the nine withdrew after the reduced schedule had begun: four in the first month and three in the second. In exit forms, six of the nine gave workload or inability to maintain output as the main reason, and two gave scheduling. The organisations that found the change hardest were therefore removed from the sample before the outcome was measured. With nine of 70 organisations missing, and those nine plausibly the least successful, the reported sample of 61 is a sample of survivors.

## 2. The output measure

The primary outcome was an index completed by a manager who was also the pilot's internal sponsor. Managers were asked to base the index on organisational records, but were not required to submit them. Twenty-three organisations did submit underlying records (billable hours delivered, tickets closed, units produced, or cases completed). For these 23 we can compare the manager's index with the index implied by the records.

**Table 1. Manager-reported and record-based output, 23 organisations with records**

| Measure | Mean output index (baseline = 100) |
|---|---|
| Manager-reported index | 98.9 |
| Index computed from submitted records | 95.1 |
| Difference | −3.8 points |

In 19 of the 23 organisations the manager-reported index exceeded the record-based index. We do not suggest bad faith. A manager responsible for a change he or she advocated, asked to rate its effect on a scale where 100 means "unchanged", will tend to round toward success. But the difference is systematic, and the headline output figure of 98.7 should not be taken at face value.

## 3. The hours denominator

The pilot computed output per hour by dividing output by the ratio of scheduled hours, 0.8. Twenty-seven organisations used time-tracking software throughout. Their data show average actual weekly hours of 40.3 at baseline and 34.6 during the pilot, a fall of 14.1% rather than 20%. The difference comes from two sources visible in the logs: longer working days on the remaining four days (average +0.7 hours per day), and work logged on the scheduled day off (on average 1.6 hours per week). Some further work on the day off is probably not logged.

Seventeen organisations have both submitted output records and time tracking. In this subset, record-based output was 95.4 and actual hours fell from 40.4 to 34.8 (−13.9%). The implied gain in output per actual hour is 10.8% (95.4 / 86.1), less than half the reported 23.4%.

**Table 2. Implied gain in output per hour under successive corrections**

| Specification | Output | Hours ratio | Gain per hour |
|---|---|---|---|
| As reported (all 61) | 98.7 | 0.800 | +23.4% |
| Record-based output, scheduled hours (23) | 95.1 | 0.800 | +18.9% |
| Manager-reported output, actual hours (27) | 98.4 | 0.859 | +14.6% |
| Record-based output, actual hours (17) | 95.4 | 0.861 | +10.8% |

## 4. Revenue

The working paper reports revenue 1.4% higher than in the previous year. This is a nominal comparison. Consumer prices rose by 4.1% over the same twelve months; in real terms, revenue in participating organisations fell by approximately 2.6%. Revenue is in any case a poor proxy for productivity, but the figure as presented gives a misleading impression of growth.

## 5. Sectoral claims

The pilot concluded that gains in output per hour were "found in every sector" and that the model is "sector-general". This conclusion is an artifact of the per-hour metric. When hours are cut by 20%, any output index above 80 will register as a per-hour gain. Retail and hospitality output fell by 6.9% on the manager-reported measure; the three retail and hospitality organisations among the 23 with records show a fall of 11.2%. A fall in output of this size in a customer-facing business is not evidence that reduced hours work there. The Varden County trial's counter and contact-centre stratum, the only randomised evidence on coverage-bound work, found a fall in output per employee of 11.4% and longer waits for the public. That is, in our view, the most reliable finding in the literature to date.

## 6. Novelty

After the corrections above, a gain in output per actual hour of about 11% remains in the subset of survivors with usable data. We think this residual should not be read as a durable effect. The pilot's own survey shows self-reported energy at work rising by 0.61 standard deviations at month three and falling to 0.29 at month six. Extrapolating this decline, energy would return to baseline at around month ten. A change that staff chose, welcomed and knew to be under evaluation is the classic setting for a novelty effect: effort rises while the change is new and observed, and falls back once it is routine. Six months is not long enough to distinguish a novelty effect from a durable one, and the burden of proof lies with those claiming the latter.

## 7. The meetings hypothesis

The Varden trial's authors report, in an unregistered exploratory analysis, that cuts in recurring meetings correlated with per-hour gains across seven treated offices, and suggest this as a mechanism. We regard this as a post hoc account fitted to a subgroup. A correlation across seven offices, selected for analysis after the results were known, is precisely the kind of finding that does not replicate. The meetings explanation has an intuitive appeal that has outrun its evidence, and it should not be cited as a mechanism.

## 8. Conclusion

Taking the problems together: attrition removed the organisations least able to cope; the output measure overstated output by roughly four points; the hours measure overstated the reduction in time by roughly six points; and the remaining gain coincides with a decaying measure of enthusiasm. We conclude that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the best-supported finding is the negative one: where output depends on presence, reduced hours reduce output.

We recommend that future evaluations use record-based output, actual hours, a randomised or at least matched comparison group, follow-up of at least eighteen months, and analysis of all enrolled organisations including those that withdraw.

## Data note

All re-analyses use the Halden pilot microdata (release 1.2). The corrections in Table 2 can only be computed for subsets of organisations, and those subsets were not chosen at random; organisations with time tracking and records may differ from the others. Our corrected estimates therefore describe those subsets, not the pilot as a whole.

response:
I've read it. Varga and Holm re-analyse the Halden microdata and find four problems:

- Withdrawals happened after the schedule started and were mostly for workload reasons, not during preparation for scheduling reasons as the working paper says.
- Manager-rated output exceeds record-based output by 3.8 points.
- Actual hours fell 14%, not 20%.
- Revenue fell in real terms.

Correcting output and hours together, in the 17 organisations where both can be done, brings the per-hour gain from 23.4% to 10.8%. They then attribute the remaining 10.8% to novelty, dismiss Varden's meetings analysis, and conclude that per-hour gains from reduced hours are "entirely an artifact."

The comment does two different things. Sections 1–5 are careful source-based correction and should carry real weight. Sections 6–8 go beyond what their evidence shows, in the same way they criticise Halden for doing.

## Arithmetic

Most of it checks out:

- Table 2: 95.1/0.8 is +18.9%, 98.4/0.859 is +14.6%, and 95.4/0.861 is +10.8%.
- Hours: 40.3→34.6 is −14.1%, and 40.4→34.8 is −13.9%.
- Revenue: 1.014/1.041 is −2.6% real.
- Sign test: 19 of 23 managers rating above records gives p ≈ 0.003, so the bias is not chance.

Two figures don't reconcile:

1. **The hours decomposition (§3) overshoots the total.** Four days at +0.7 hours is 2.8 hours. Add 1.6 hours on the day off and you get 4.4 hours over the 32 scheduled, which is 36.4 hours. The measured average is 34.6. Measured from the 40.3 baseline the gap is bigger still. Either a component is misreported or the two figures come from different subsets. This should be checked against the logs before publication.
2. **The novelty extrapolation (§6) gives month 9, not month 10.** A straight line through 0.61 SD at month 3 and 0.29 SD at month 6 falls about 0.107 SD a month and reaches zero around month 8.7. The difference doesn't matter much on its own, but see the next section on what this extrapolation can support.

## What holds, at full weight

- **Attrition (§1).** If the exit forms say what the authors report, the working paper misdescribed its own withdrawals, and that is a serious problem. Six of nine left citing workload, mostly after the schedule began. Halden's authors should respond directly. The comment could also bound the effect with an intention-to-treat analysis, for example assuming withdrawn organisations had output of 80, meaning no per-hour gain.
- **The output measure (§2).** A systematic gap of about 4 points, in the direction you'd expect from managers who sponsored the change, is a solid finding. They frame it fairly, without alleging bad faith.
- **Hours and revenue (§3–4).** These confirm with data what was only suspected about the Halden paper. The 10.8% figure is the best estimate available for Halden, and they're appropriately clear in the Data note that it applies to a non-random subset.
- **Sectors (§5).** The point that the per-hour metric guarantees a gain whenever output stays above 80 is correct. Retail output fell, and Varden's counter stratum points the same way.

## Where it overreaches

**1. "Entirely an artifact" goes against their own numbers.** Their corrections leave a 10.8% gain. The step from 10.8% to zero rests entirely on §6, which has three weaknesses:

- **It extrapolates two points of self-reported energy.** Energy is not output, and two points give no evidence that the decline is linear.
- **The direct test is in their hands and they don't run it.** Halden's output index was monthly. If output per actual hour declined across months 1–6 in the 17-organisation subset, that would support novelty. If it didn't, that would count against it.
- **"Burden of proof" means the question is open, not settled.** Saying the burden lies with those claiming a durable effect is a reasonable stance. But it implies that whether the 10.8% lasts is undecided. It does not license concluding that the gain is zero.

So the comment converts an open question into a negative answer. That is a mirror image of Halden turning one into a positive one.

**2. They cite Varden selectively.** §5 calls Varden's counter stratum "the most reliable finding in the literature." It does not mention Varden's case-processing stratum. That stratum had the same randomised design, with record-based output and timesheet hours, and found output per employee essentially unchanged while actual hours fell 13%. That is a per-hour gain of up to 12.5%.

Randomisation, administrative output and measured hours together rule out three of the comment's four explanations (selection, the output measure, the hours denominator). Only novelty remains, and Varden ran for nine months with a control group that also knew about the trial. To support "entirely an artifact," the comment would have to explain away this result, and it doesn't engage with it at all. Varden's result has caveats: overtime pay and unclaimed hours may mean the gain is overstated. But they reduce its size. They don't make it disappear.

**3. §7 attacks a claim Varden didn't make.** Varden called the meetings analysis unregistered and exploratory, said that a correlation across seven offices "cannot establish a mechanism," and registered a confirmatory test. The comment's characterisation differs in three ways:

- **"Suggest this as a mechanism."** Varden said it might account for part of the gain if confirmed, which is a weaker claim.
- **"A subgroup."** The seven offices are all the treated offices in a stratum defined before randomisation. They weren't selected.
- **"Selected for analysis after the results were known."** According to Varden, the meetings data were collected in month six at managers' request, before the nine-month results.

The correct status is "unestablished, test pending," and that is what Varden said. Telling readers the hypothesis "should not be cited as a mechanism" is fair. Treating it as refuted is not. It also matters for the comment's own argument: meetings reform is the main alternative to novelty as an explanation for the remaining gain, and dismissing it leaves novelty looking like the only option.

**4. The conclusion is broader than the Data note allows.** The Data note says the corrected estimates describe subsets, not the pilot as a whole. The conclusion then makes a claim about "reduced-hours schemes" in general, based on a single pilot plus one stratum of one trial.

## What the evidence now supports

Taking Halden, Varden and this comment together:

- **Coverage-bound work:** reduced hours lower output per employee and worsen service. This is well supported and can be treated as settled.
- **Halden's headline gain:** 23.4% was inflated. About 11% survives correction in a non-random subset. This holds, given the source check.
- **Backlog and office work:** output per employee holds roughly steady, and output per actual hour rises. On the best evidence (Varden), the rise is around 10–12% at most. This is supported, and cost per output unit including overtime is still unreported.
- **Whether the per-hour gain lasts:** open. Halden's monthly output trajectory and Varden's 24-month follow-up would settle it.
- **Why it happens (rest, meetings, novelty):** open. Varden's registered confirmatory test addresses meetings.

## Suggested revisions to the comment

1. Reconcile the hours decomposition in §3 with the 34.6-hour total.
2. Add a month-by-month analysis of output per actual hour to test novelty directly, and run the energy extrapolation correctly.
3. Engage with Varden's case-processing result.
4. Correct the description of Varden's meetings analysis in §7.
5. Replace "entirely an artifact" with a claim matching Table 2 and the Data note. For example: "about half of Halden's reported gain is attributable to measurement; whether the remainder is durable is untested."
6. Add an intention-to-treat bound for the withdrawals.

Points 1–5 of the comment should stand as written. Its corrections to Halden are the most useful contribution in this exchange so far. I can draft this as a referee report.
